category.name: Social & Platform Research
category.description: Searching, monitoring and analysing content on social platforms. This category has degraded severely since 2023 as platforms closed research access, and several once-standard tools no longer exist. What follows reflects what is actually available now, not what the training material still recommends.

tools.name: Meta Content Library
tools.summary: Meta's gated research access to Facebook and Instagram public content — the successor to CrowdTangle.
tools.description:
The Meta Content Library provides approved researchers with search and analysis over public content from Facebook and Instagram, through a web interface and an API. It is the designated replacement for CrowdTangle, which Meta shut down on 14 August 2024 despite sustained objection from researchers, civil society organisations, journalists and legislators.

It is catalogued here because it is the only sanctioned route to this data, not because it is a good replacement. Independent assessment by Proof News, the Tow Center for Digital Journalism and the Algorithmic Transparency Institute found the replacement less transparent and less accessible than CrowdTangle, with fewer features across eleven key areas of capability, a cumbersome and slow access process, and only a small fraction of CrowdTangle's user base successfully onboarded. Many journalists cannot get access at all.

Plan accordingly. If your work depends on Facebook or Instagram data, treat access as a months-long institutional process with an uncertain outcome, and design your method so that a refusal does not end the investigation.
tools.costNotes: No fee, but access is gated by an application and eligibility assessment. Eligibility has centred on academic and non-profit researchers with institutional affiliation; independent journalists have reported substantial difficulty qualifying. Access is granted through an approved partner process rather than self-service signup.
tools.legalNotes: Access is governed by a research agreement with real constraints on what may be done with the data, how it must be stored, and what may be published — read it, because it binds you and your institution. The data concerns identifiable individuals, and the agreement's terms sit on top of, not instead of, your own data-protection obligations. Circumventing the sanctioned route by scraping Meta platforms breaches their terms of service and has been litigated aggressively.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The data comes from the platform itself and is authoritative as to what the platform holds. The limitations are access and scope: reduced feature coverage relative to CrowdTangle, restricted fields, and gated availability mean many research questions that were answerable in 2023 are not answerable now. Absence of a finding may reflect the tool's constraints rather than the world.
tools.confidenceNotes: The 14 August 2024 CrowdTangle shutdown and the Content Library's status as its replacement were confirmed during this review, along with the documented independent findings on reduced capability and restricted access. The precise current eligibility criteria were not verified against Meta's own application page.

tools.name: X Advanced Search
tools.summary: Native advanced search on X with date, account, engagement and geographic operators.
tools.description:
X's own advanced search remains the most practical way to search the platform, offering operators for date ranges, from and to specific accounts, replies and mentions, minimum engagement thresholds, language, and media type. The date-range operators are the ones that matter most for verification: bounding a search to the hours around an event finds the earliest posts of a piece of content.

The honest framing is that this is the diminished remnant of what used to be a research-friendly platform. TweetDeck, long the standard monitoring interface, became a paid feature. The free API tier was effectively eliminated in 2023 and academic research access was withdrawn, which ended a large body of ongoing research. Third-party clients and archives were shut down.

What remains is manual search in a browser, increasingly gated behind login and rate limits that change without notice. It still works, and for finding the first appearance of a viral post it is often irreplaceable, but treat coverage as unreliable and results as non-reproducible — the same query run twice can return different results.
tools.costNotes: Search through the web interface is free but increasingly requires a logged-in account, and rate limits are applied and changed without notice. Enhanced features including the successor to TweetDeck sit behind paid subscription tiers. The developer API is paid at tiers widely reported as prohibitive for research; the previous free and academic tiers were withdrawn in 2023.
tools.legalNotes: Terms of service prohibit automated scraping and the platform has enforced this. Using a research account rather than a personal one is sound practice for both opsec and account safety. Content about identifiable individuals collected into a dataset is personal data with the usual obligations. Note that viewing a profile while logged in can, depending on platform features and settings, be visible to that account.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Search coverage is demonstrably incomplete and inconsistent — identical queries return different results at different times, older content is unreliably indexed, and deleted or restricted accounts vanish from results entirely. A negative result carries almost no evidential weight. Capture and archive anything you find immediately, because you may not be able to find it again. Rated 2 for reproducibility, not for the value of what it does return.
tools.confidenceNotes: The advanced search interface exists and is used daily, but this platform has changed access rules, rate limits and URLs repeatedly and with no notice since 2022, and its current gating behaviour was not verified in this review. Expect the specifics in this entry to age faster than any other in the catalogue.

tools.name: TGStat
tools.summary: Telegram channel analytics and search — subscriber trends, reach, post history and cross-channel citation.
tools.description:
TGStat indexes public Telegram channels and provides analytics on them: subscriber growth over time, post reach, citation between channels, and searchable post history. It also allows keyword search across indexed channels, which Telegram's own client does poorly.

Telegram matters disproportionately in conflict monitoring, extremism research and disinformation work, and its native search is weak, so an external index is close to essential. The citation graph — which channels repost which — is genuinely valuable for mapping how a narrative propagates and which channels seed it.

Two things to weigh. The operator is Russian-language and Russian-oriented, which is both why its coverage of the relevant channel ecosystem is good and a real operational-security consideration for anyone researching Russian state-adjacent activity: assume your queries are logged. Detailed data requires a paid subscription, and payment has reportedly been difficult or impossible with cards issued in the US and various other countries.
tools.costNotes: Basic channel information and search are available free. Detailed analytics, historical data and API access require a paid subscription. Payment with cards issued in the United States and some other countries has been reported as not working. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Operator jurisdiction is a genuine operational-security concern: assume search queries are retained and potentially accessible to Russian state authorities. For investigations touching Russian interests, dissidents or sanctioned entities, weigh that before querying, and consider whether an account and network that do not identify you are necessary. Indexed channel content includes personal data and, in extremism research, material that may itself be unlawful to possess in some jurisdictions.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Good coverage of the public Russian-language Telegram ecosystem and reasonable elsewhere, but indexing is incomplete and channels can be absent, delayed or removed. Metrics such as reach are platform-derived estimates, not measurements. Free-tier data is truncated in ways that can mislead about completeness. Corroborate any critical post against the channel itself and archive it.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as operational and heavily used in 2026, with a paid tier required for detailed data and reported payment difficulties for cards from the US and elsewhere. Specific pricing was not verified.

tools.name: 4CAT Capture and Analysis Toolkit
tools.summary: Self-hosted research tool for capturing and analysing datasets from social platforms and imageboards.
tools.description:
4CAT, from the Digital Methods Initiative at the University of Amsterdam, is a self-hosted research platform: you install it, capture datasets from supported sources, and run a library of analyses over them — word frequency and collocation, hashtag and URL co-occurrence, network graphs, time series, image analysis and topic clustering.

Two properties make it valuable where commercial tools are not. It is self-hosted, so your dataset and your research questions stay on your infrastructure rather than a vendor's. And it is designed for reproducibility: datasets and processing pipelines are preserved so another researcher can check your work, which is the standard academic publication requires and most OSINT tooling cannot meet.

It has notably strong support for imageboards and fringe platforms that mainstream tools ignore but that matter for studying how narratives originate. Limits: it requires real infrastructure and technical setup, and its data sources are subject to the same platform restrictions as everything else — sources break as platforms close access, and the currently working set should be checked against the project's documentation rather than assumed.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source, self-hosted. Costs are your own infrastructure and setup time. Some data sources require your own API credentials, which may themselves be paid.
tools.legalNotes: Self-hosting means you are the controller of every dataset it captures, with full responsibility for lawful basis, security, retention and deletion — an advantage for confidentiality and an obligation you cannot delegate. Capturing from platforms may breach their terms of service depending on the source and method used; the research-exemption position varies by jurisdiction and is not universal. Datasets of social media posts about identifiable people are personal data at scale and should have a defined retention period from the outset.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well-engineered and academically maintained, with reproducibility as an explicit design goal. Reliability of any given data source depends on that platform's current access policy, and sources degrade or break without the tool being at fault. Analyses are only as sound as the dataset's construction — a biased capture produces confident, wrong conclusions, and 4CAT will not warn you.
tools.confidenceNotes: The project is real and academically maintained, but its currently functioning data sources change continuously with platform policy and were not verified during this review. Check the project documentation for which sources actually work before planning around it.

tools.name: Social Blade
tools.summary: Historical statistics on social accounts across several platforms — follower trends and growth anomalies.
tools.description:
Social Blade tracks public statistics for accounts on YouTube, Twitch, Instagram, X and other platforms, retaining daily history of follower counts, view counts and upload frequency.

The investigative use is anomaly detection. Organic accounts grow in characteristic patterns; purchased followers and coordinated amplification do not. A step change of tens of thousands of followers overnight, or growth that stops dead when a campaign ends, is visible in the history and invisible in the current profile. It is also the easiest way to establish when an account actually became prominent, which frequently contradicts the narrative around it.

Limits: it tracks accounts it has been asked to track, so history for an account may begin only when someone first looked it up — and an account with no history is not necessarily new. Coverage and metric availability vary a lot by platform and have degraded as platforms restricted public statistics. Data is scraped from public profiles and inherits any platform-side inaccuracy.
tools.costNotes: Free access to most historical statistics with advertising. Paid tiers remove advertising and add extended history, exports and API access. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Aggregates publicly displayed account statistics. Statistics about an individual's account are personal data when the account identifies a person, though this is at the low-sensitivity end. Publishing an inference that an account bought followers is an allegation requiring more than a growth chart.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Useful and often the only source for historical account statistics, but it is a scraper: gaps, tracking start dates that postdate the account, and platform changes that break collection are all common. A suspicious growth curve is a strong lead and not proof of inauthentic behaviour — platforms also purge bots, run recommendation experiments and change how counts are computed, all of which produce step changes.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established service. Not fetched during this review; per-platform metric availability changes as platforms restrict public data.

tools.name: Pushshift
tools.summary: Historical Reddit archive, restricted since 2023 to verified Reddit moderators for moderation purposes only.
tools.description:
Pushshift was for years the archive that made Reddit research possible: a complete, searchable, bulk-downloadable corpus of Reddit submissions and comments including content later edited or deleted. An enormous amount of published research on online communities depended on it.

It is listed here principally so that investigators reading older guides understand why it does not work for them. Following Reddit's API changes in 2023, Pushshift access was restricted to Reddit moderators who register, are individually approved by Reddit, and use it only for moderation purposes on communities they moderate. There is no public API, no general developer access and no bulk historical access for researchers.

If you are not a moderator with an approved application, this tool is unavailable to you, and any workflow that assumes otherwise needs redesigning. Third-party successors offering historical Reddit data exist and are frequently recommended, but their legal footing, data provenance and durability were not established during this review and none is catalogued here on that basis.
tools.costNotes: No fee, but access is restricted. Reddit moderators must register a Pushshift account and obtain explicit approval from Reddit, with use limited to moderation of communities they moderate. Requests are submitted through a designated Reddit process and are prioritised toward moderators of substantial, rule-abiding communities.
tools.legalNotes: Access is conditioned on a moderation purpose and using approved access for research or investigation would breach those conditions. The archive historically included content users had deleted, which raises a real ethical question about processing material a person actively withdrew — an erasure request under GDPR is not answered by 'it was public when we collected it'.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The historical corpus was comprehensive and well regarded for the period it covered. Its reliability for present-day work is dominated by the access restriction rather than data quality: for almost every user of this catalogue it is simply unavailable. Marked accordingly.
tools.confidenceNotes: The post-2023 restriction to verified Reddit moderators for moderation purposes only, with individual Reddit approval and no public, developer or bulk access, was confirmed during this review. Catalogued as materially restricted rather than omitted, so that users of older guides understand the change.

tools.name: YouTube Data API
tools.summary: Google's official API for YouTube metadata — video, channel and playlist details with precise timestamps.
tools.description:
The YouTube Data API provides structured access to public metadata: video titles, descriptions, tags, exact publication timestamps, channel creation dates, subscriber and view counts, playlists and, subject to configuration, comment threads.

For verification the crucial field is the precise publication timestamp. Establishing that a video was published before a claimed event is often decisive in debunking recycled footage, and the API returns that timestamp to the second in a stated time zone, which the web interface's relative dates ('2 years ago') do not. Channel creation dates are similarly useful for assessing whether an account is what it claims to be.

This capability matters more now that Amnesty International's YouTube DataViewer — the tool most verification training still recommends for exactly this purpose — can no longer be confirmed as operating; it is not catalogued here for that reason. The API is the durable route to the same information.

Limits: it needs a Google Cloud project and an API key, it operates on a daily quota that ordinary use can exhaust surprisingly quickly, and it returns only what YouTube exposes publicly.
tools.costNotes: Free within a default daily quota, requiring a Google account and a Google Cloud project with the API enabled. Quota increases are requested through an application process. Different operations consume different quota amounts, and search is markedly more expensive than direct lookups.
tools.legalNotes: Governed by the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, which impose real constraints on storage, caching duration and permitted uses of retrieved data — read them before building anything that retains results. Metadata about identifiable channel owners is personal data. Using the official API is the terms-compliant alternative to scraping, and is preferable for that reason alone.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative platform-sourced metadata; the publication timestamp is the platform's own record and is the strongest available evidence of when a video appeared on YouTube. Two caveats: it records upload to YouTube, not creation of the footage, and a video can be uploaded long after it was filmed or re-uploaded after deletion. Counts are approximate by design and refreshed on Google's schedule.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, documented Google API. Not fetched during this review; quota costs and terms change periodically and should be read before building against it.
